title: The Basement Prison at Stanford
text:
In August 1971 the psychologist Philip Zimbardo turned a basement corridor of the Stanford psychology building into a mock prison. Two dozen male students, screened as healthy and stable, were paid to take part and were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners. Prisoners were "arrested" at home, given smocks and numbers, and locked in small cells. Guards received uniforms, sticks and mirrored sunglasses. Zimbardo himself acted as prison superintendent.

Within days some guards became harsh. They woke prisoners at night for counts, made them do push-ups, removed mattresses and used solitary confinement in a closet. Several prisoners broke down and were released early. The study, planned for two weeks, was stopped after six days, after Christina Maslach, a young psychologist who visited the basement, objected strongly to what she saw.

For decades the study was taught as proof that roles alone turn ordinary people cruel. Later work told a more complicated story. Recordings and interviews released over the years show that the research team briefed the guards on creating fear and encouraged them to be "tough," and that some guards were acting a part. Only a minority behaved abusively, while others stayed fair.
lesson: The tone a leader sets, through what they encourage, permit and ignore, shapes how people with power behave. Watching passively from the top is itself a choice.
people: Craig Haney, Curtis Banks, Philip Zimbardo
source: Haney, C., Banks, C., and Zimbardo, P. (1973). Interpersonal dynamics in a simulated prison. International Journal of Criminology and Penology, 1, 69-97.
caveat: The study had no real control group, and later critiques (notably by Thibault Le Texier in 2018) show guards were coached, so it is not clean evidence that roles alone cause cruelty.
